lesson.title: Switches that decide
lesson.subtitle: AND, OR and NOT, built from switches

video.title: Switches that decide
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma — your maths teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma in a hot classroom after lunch, pointing up at a ceiling fan; a few students fan themselves with exercise books.
scenes.animation: Fan blades still; a thermometer rises; a question mark pops over the fan.
scenes.narration: Our classroom fan has a rule. It should run when it's hot and someone is in the room. But a switch can't think. So how does a machine follow a rule?

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: switches that decide, with AND, OR and NOT.

scenes.visual: A big light switch flips on and off; a 1 and a 0 appear beside it in turn.
scenes.narration: A switch is either on or off. Computers write on as one, and off as zero. Every decision a device makes is built from ones and zeros like these.

scenes.visual: A battery, a bulb and two switches, A and B, one after the other in a single loop. Both close: the bulb lights. A opens: dark.
scenes.animation: Switches close one by one; the bulb lights only on the second; A flips open and the light dies.
scenes.narration: Put two switches one after the other in the loop: that's called series. The light comes on only when switch A and switch B are both on. Turn either off, and the loop breaks. That's AND.

scenes.visual: The same bulb with switches A and B on two branches side by side. Either one closing lights the bulb.
scenes.animation: Current dots take the upper path, then the lower one; the bulb stays lit.
scenes.narration: Now put them side by side: that's parallel, and the current has two paths. The light comes on when A or B is on, or both. That's OR.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor at his bench with a lamp on two parallel switches: A open, B closed. Two answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Two switches in parallel. Switch A is off, and switch B is on. Is the lamp on or off?

scenes.visual: The lamp glows; current dots run through switch B's branch while A's branch stays empty.
scenes.animation: Dots flow through B; the lamp glows.
scenes.narration: It's on. Switch B gives the current a path, so the loop is closed. With OR, one is enough; with AND, you'd need both.

scenes.visual: A fridge door closes on a small button and the inside light goes off; the door opens, the button pops out, the light comes on.
scenes.animation: Door swings shut and open; the light follows the opposite of the button.
scenes.narration: The third one is NOT: it flips its input. Think of a fridge. A shut door presses a button, and the light goes off. The light is on when the button is NOT pressed.

scenes.visual: A four-row table builds itself on a board: A, B and the light, with 0s and 1s; the last row lights up.
scenes.animation: Rows write in one by one; the 1 in the last row glows.
scenes.narration: To check a rule, make a truth table: every possible input, and the output. Two switches give four rows. For AND, the output is one only when both are on.

scenes.visual: A classroom wall with a thermometer and a motion sensor wired to a small box marked AND, then to OR with a wall switch, then to the fan.
scenes.animation: Each input lights as it is named; the fan spins at the end.
scenes.narration: Now our fan. One input comes from a temperature sensor: is it hot? Another comes from a motion sensor: is someone in? Hot AND someone in turns the fan on. And the teacher's own switch joins with OR, so she can always switch it on.

scenes.visual: Amina beside a school water tank on a stand, a pipe running down to a well with a small pump. Two rule cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A pump fills the school tank from a well. It should run when the tank is low, but never when the well is dry. Which rule: low AND NOT dry, or low OR dry?

scenes.visual: Four cards line up: two switches in a row, two side by side, a flip arrow, a small table.
scenes.narration: Low AND NOT dry: the pump runs only when the tank needs water and the well has some. Remember: series makes AND, parallel makes OR, NOT flips, and a truth table checks every case.

scenes.visual: A student at a kitchen table with a notebook: a drawing of a fridge, its rule, and a four-row table; a battery, a bulb and foil strips beside it.
scenes.animation: The rule writes itself; the table fills row by row.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: pick a device at home, like a fridge or a torch, and write its rule with AND, OR or NOT. Then make its truth table. Got a battery, a bulb and foil? Build AND and OR for real. Next time: counting in ones and zeros.

checkpoints.prompt: Two switches are in parallel. A is off and B is on. Is the lamp on?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — in parallel, one closed path is enough, and B gives one. That's OR.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — in parallel, the current needs only one path. B is on, so the lamp is on: that's OR.

checkpoints.prompt: A pump should run when the tank is low, but never when the well is dry. Which rule?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — it runs only when the tank needs water AND the well is NOT dry.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — with OR, the pump would run whenever the well is dry, and burn out. It needs low AND NOT dry.
